2. E-13b — F31 closure

Finding

R0.8.4 changes the incarnation lock from:

<caller-chosen-root>.lock

to:

<deployment-anchor>/<LocusId>/incarnation.lock

The root path no longer chooses the currentness namespace.

NC24 copies:

store
root

byte-for-byte to different pathnames while both controllers share one deployment anchor. Exactly one controller becomes current; the loser does not advance and its mutation is refused.

The control also correctly avoids assuming whether A or B wins the OS-lock race.

Ruling

The specific F31 defect is CLOSED under this profile:

single host
one protected deployment-owned anchor namespace
one LocusId -> one incarnation lock

Recommended evidence classification:

E-13a same-anchor exclusivity:
    TESTED

E-13b canonical host-local Locus currentness:
    TESTED-CONDITIONAL / CLOSED-F31
    condition:
        deployment anchor namespace is trusted, canonical, and not
        attacker-selectable / attacker-replaceable

E-13c external witnessed multi-namespace currentness:
    TESTED under ARM-B single-witness profile

Do not promote E-13b to an unqualified universal theorem.

The repaired code itself correctly admits the boundary:

an attacker who can choose another anchor namespace has another deployment; cross-machine uniqueness is not claimed.

That is good epistemic discipline.

Remaining trust-boundary issue

F22 is still open and is related.

Currentness now depends on a deployment filesystem namespace. Therefore the deployment-owned directory/anchor identity itself belongs in the trusted-substrate profile.

The next layer question is not “is the lock keyed by root path?” — that is fixed.

It is:

can an attacker who is not authorized to replace the canonical deployment anchor nevertheless redirect/replace one of the filesystem objects that the trusted anchor depends on?

That should be handled by the R0.8.5 / F22 work, not by reopening F31.

3. E-14 — F23/F24 closure

What R0.8.4 repaired

Canonical material now includes ordered rows from:

SELECT type, name, tbl_name, sql
FROM sqlite_schema
ORDER BY type, name

and the canonical encoding tag moves to v3.

Additionally, on each open R0.8.4:

  • WAL mode is requested and its returned value is asserted;

  • SQLITE_DBCONFIG_DEFENSIVE = true;

  • SQLITE_DBCONFIG_TRUSTED_SCHEMA = false;

  • schema is part of the canonical material;

  • CanonicalMutation carries the same schema contract rather than re-reading a potentially changed interpretation during projection;

  • genesis adopts the store's schema-bound canonical head exactly once under strict preconditions.

This directly addresses the reproduced F23 attacks:

schema-only collation edit invisible to digest
schema-induced binding destruction
trigger mutating canonical state inside the honest writer transaction

Ruling

The specific F23/F24 defects are CLOSED under a trusted/fixed SQLite interpreter profile.

Recommended E-14 classification:

TESTED-CONDITIONAL

condition:
    the SQLite engine / collation implementations / database configuration
    that interpret sqlite_schema are part of the trusted execution profile

committed:
    schema objects represented in sqlite_schema
    canonical row values
    canonical ordering contract

not claimed:
    adversarial replacement of the SQLite engine binary itself
    arbitrary hostile custom collation/function implementation outside the
    declared runtime trust profile

I would remove FALSIFIED-OPEN for the specific F23/F24 attacks once the R0.8.4 receipt is admitted, but retain CONDITIONAL rather than calling E-14 universally closed.

The deeper principle remains:

committing interpreter-produced values is insufficient unless the interpretation contract is either committed or explicitly trusted.

R0.8.4 now does both in a reasonable way for this profile: schema is committed; the SQLite engine is trusted.

  • carries the canonical schema through mutation projection.

Ruling

    + committed schema contract
    + defensive configuration

This is stronger than the v2.4 pre-adjudication status.

6. FAC-CONTROL-SENSITIVITY — ACCEPT as a factory evidence rule

R0.8.4 produced multiple examples of controls / runners that could print PASS while not measuring what their receipt claimed:

  • wrong semantic gate;

  • assuming which process wins a race;

  • demanding root motion when the correct behavior is refusal;

  • a value compared to itself;

  • jq // erasing false;

  • PIPESTATUS captured incorrectly;

  • shell quoting causing a leg to execute nothing while returning success.

This deserves a first-class rule.

Recommended location

Put it in the factory / evidence-admissibility lane, not in S1–S5.

Suggested form:

FAC-CONTROL-SENSITIVITY

A control may promote an evidence class only if its sensitivity to the
claimed forbidden state is itself evidenced.

At least one of:

A. pre-fix or injected-fault execution demonstrates FAIL;
B. an independent witness demonstrates that the control reaches the
   intended subject and discriminates the forbidden state;
C. a mutation/negative-control pair proves that removing the target
   mechanism flips the verdict.

A green-only control with no demonstrated failure sensitivity cannot
support promotion.

Also add an instrument-self-check corollary:

the runner/receipt machinery that records a control must itself have a
negative control capable of making the aggregate fail

R0.8.4's falsify-before-repair sequence is an excellent first witness family.

I would classify this as:

factory epistemic invariant / evidence-admission rule

not a runtime semantic invariant.

7. L1? — keep, but correct the witness claim

The candidate itself is worthwhile:

L1? Recoverable succession / explicit terminalization

and it should remain on a separate liveness axis.

However, the current finite witness does not prove the statement as written if the statement uses temporal language such as:

eventually resolves

What the current model actually proves

For every modeled evidenced-loss state, it checks:

there EXISTS a path
to:
    successor at a later generation
    OR explicit terminal state

That is:

resolution reachability
resolvability
absence of a dead-end evidenced state

It is not:

all fair executions eventually resolve

because the model contains no scheduler/fairness semantics. An enabled finalize or terminalize action can simply be postponed forever in an unconstrained execution.

Required correction

Either:

Option A — weaken the current witness claim

Call the current result:

L1-PRE / resolution availability

From every admissibly evidenced permanent-loss state,
a safety-preserving resolution path exists.

This is exactly what the script proves.

Then later add temporal liveness.

Option B — state an explicit fairness assumption

For example:

Under weak fairness for continuously enabled finality actions,
every admissibly evidenced permanent-loss state eventually reaches
exactly one later-generation successor or an explicit terminal state.

Then model-check the temporal property with an actual transition-system / Büchi / TLA+ / TLC-style fairness semantics rather than existential BFS.

My recommendation

Use Option A now.

Keep L1? as the semantic liveness candidate, but label the Python witness:

EXHAUSTIVE-IN-FINITE-MODEL:
    resolution is reachable from every evidenced state

NOT YET PROVEN:
    temporal eventuality under a scheduler/fairness model

Then build the smallest possible TLA+/explicit-state temporal model for L1 before production finality changes.

This avoids smuggling fairness into the word "eventually."
